127.title: Savitri's vow
127.hook: Savitri fasts three nights, then follows Death; why a Hindu fast is a vow
127.carry: a fast is a vow, chosen with love
127.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows that often include fasting, on particular weekdays, festivals or lunar days (and some married women keep Vat Savitri, honoring Savitri's vow): some eat only fruit and milk, some one meal, some abstain from grains, and a few go without water; children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanuman grabbed at the sun, then bowed to it as his teacher. Your line was surya namaskar is a bow to the sun.

segments.voice: A princess named Savitri chooses her own husband: Satyavan, an exiled prince living in the forest. Then a sage warns her: he will die in exactly one year. She marries him anyway, and counts the days. Three days before the end, she makes a vow. For three days and nights she will fast and stand, without rest. On the last morning she follows Satyavan into the forest. He lays his head in her lap. And Yama, the lord of death, walks out of the trees with his noose.
screen: `ONE YEAR TO LIVE.` → `SHE MARRIES HIM ANYWAY.` → `THREE NIGHTS OF FASTING.` → `DEATH WALKS OUT OF THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Yama takes Satyavan's life, and Savitri follows him. He tells her to turn back. She keeps walking, and speaks so wisely that he offers her gifts, anything but her husband's life. Sight for her blind father-in-law. His lost kingdom. Sons for her own father. Then she asks for a hundred sons, by Satyavan. Yama grants it, and now he has to give Satyavan back. That's the Mahabharata's story. In parts of India married women still keep a fast for Savitri, called Vat Savitri, at a banyan tree. Her three nights were a vrata: a vow. That's the teaching. In Hindu practice a fast is often one way of keeping a vow, a promise made for a purpose, for a set time, often to a form of God. Mondays, for many, are for Shiva. The nine nights of Navaratri. And in three days you'll meet the eleventh day of the moon. Ways to keep one differ: only fruit and milk, one simple meal, no grains, and at the strictest, no water. Another word for fasting, upavasa, is explained as staying near: near God, near the purpose. The hunger becomes a bell. Every time your stomach speaks, you remember why you chose this. Children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused, because a fast that harms the body breaks the line from two days ago: the body is a temple. So when a coworker skips the office pizza for her Monday fast, she isn't being punished. She's keeping a promise, chosen, with love.

segments.voice: No fasting required, and if food is complicated for you, leave food out of this completely. Choose one small thing to skip for the rest of today: a snack, sugar in your tea, or something that isn't food at all, like an hour of scrolling. Then give it a purpose. If you pray, offer it to the form of God you love. If you don't, offer it for someone you love, the way Savitri did. When you miss it later, let that bring you back.

128.title: Krishna's dinner at Vidura's
128.hook: Krishna turns down a palace feast for a meal given with love; sattvic food
128.carry: sattvic food: simple, and given with love
128.howItsDone: Many Hindus aim for sattvic meals, fresh, simple and often vegetarian, cooked with a calm mind and offered to God before eating; some also avoid onion, garlic and alcohol, especially on festival days, fast days or in temple kitchens; practices differ widely by family and community.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri fasted three nights and followed Death. Your line was a fast is a vow, chosen with love.

segments.voice: Krishna rides into the capital as a messenger of peace, trying to stop a war between cousins. Prince Duryodhana, who wants that war, has laid out a royal welcome: rich dishes, fine seats, every comfort. Krishna won't eat a bite. A guest eats someone's food for one of two reasons, he says: because there is love, or because he is in need. You have no love for me, and I'm not in need. Then he walks to the house of Vidura, his honest friend, and eats there, gladly.
screen: `A ROYAL FEAST.` → `KRISHNA WON'T TOUCH IT.` → `LOVE, OR NEED.` → `DINNER AT VIDURA'S.`

segments.voice: That's the Mahabharata. Families still retell it, sometimes with extra loving details of their own. The teaching under it runs all through Hindu kitchens: food carries more than taste. Krishna himself sorts the world into three qualities, the gunas. Sattva is clarity, balance, light. Rajas is drive and restlessness. Tamas is heaviness and dullness. And he sorts food the same way. Sattvic food, he says, is fresh, wholesome and nourishing, and increases life, strength, health and joy. Rajasic food is too sour, too salty, too hot and burning, and brings pain and unease. Tamasic food is stale, spoiled, or left over too long. In practice, sattvic is often taken to mean fresh, simple, vegetarian meals, and some also skip onion and garlic. Families and communities differ, and not every Hindu is vegetarian. But many Hindus add what Krishna showed at Vidura's door: the heart of the cook and the giver goes into the meal. That's why some grandmothers won't let anyone cook angry, why temple kitchens are kept calm and clean, and why many families offer the food to God first, so it comes back as prasad. So sattvic isn't just a menu. Before you eat, ask two things. Will this leave me clearer? And was it given with love?
screen: `FOOD CARRIES MORE THAN TASTE.` · `THREE GUNAS: CLARITY, DRIVE, DULLNESS.` · `FRESH, SIMPLE, OFTEN VEGETARIAN.` · `THE COOK'S HEART GOES IN.` · then, large: `SATTVIC FOOD: SIMPLE, AND GIVEN WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: If there's a small bite near you, a piece of fruit, a nut, a sip of tea, take it now; if not, picture your next meal. Before you eat, look at it and ask where it came from and whose hands made it. If you pray, offer it silently to God first, as many Hindus do. If you don't, thank whoever made it. Then eat one bite slowly, and notice how you feel: clearer, heavier, or the same.
Sattvic. Full of sattva, clarity: simple, fresh food, given with love, that leaves the mind clear. Today's word.

129.title: Rama's naming day
129.hook: Vasishtha names four baby princes; why Hindu families mark a name, a first bite and a first haircut
129.howItsDone: Many Hindu families keep some of the samskaras: a naming ceremony, the first feeding of rice (annaprashana), the first haircut (mundan or chudakarana), often at a temple, and a first-letters ceremony honoring Saraswati.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna turned down a feast for Vidura's simple table. Your line was sattvic food: simple, and given with love.

segments.voice: Ayodhya. For years King Dasharatha has had no children. Then, after a great fire offering, his three queens give birth to four sons, and the whole city pours into the streets to celebrate. On the eleventh day, the family's sage, Vasishtha, sits with the babies to name them. The eldest: Rama, the one who brings delight. Then Bharata. Then the twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna, the slayer of enemies. A whole kingdom stops to name four babies.
screen: `NO CHILDREN, FOR YEARS.` → `FOUR SONS AT ONCE.` → `THE ELEVENTH DAY: THE NAMING.` → `RAMA, THE ONE WHO DELIGHTS.`

segments.voice: That's the Ramayana, and Vasishtha doesn't stop at names: the epic says he performed all the princes' childhood rites. Those rites are samskaras, and they're the teaching today. The word means a finishing, a polishing, the way raw metal is worked until it shines. In Hindu life, samskaras mark the steps of a person's life, from before birth to after death. Later lists often count sixteen, though the lists differ, and most families keep only some. You may have been through a few without knowing their names. Namakarana, the naming, often on the eleventh or twelfth day, like Rama's. Annaprashana, the first bite of solid food, usually rice, at around six months. Chudakarana, the first haircut, which many families call mundan, in the first or third year by family custom. A toddler wails, the barber is quick, and a grandmother catches every curl. The birth hair is shaved away, a fresh start, and many families offer it at a temple or a holy river. Vidyarambha, the start of learning: a child traces first letters, often in a plate of rice, on a day for Saraswati, the goddess of learning. It's why so many kids were taught to touch a book they've stepped on, then their forehead. And the wedding gets its own day soon. Here's what they share. Each takes an ordinary first and says: God is part of this. The child is being polished, step by step, the way a kingdom stopped for Rama. So the next time a family chat pings about a mundan, it isn't just a haircut. It's a samskara.

segments.voice: Remember a first that someone marked for you: a first day of school, a first bike ride, a birthday, a photo someone kept, and picture who was there and who made the fuss. You may only remember the story told about it, and that's fine; breathe in the fact that someone thought your small step was worth stopping for. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

130.title: Ambarisha's fast
130.hook: a king's Ekadashi, an angry sage and Vishnu's disc; the twice-monthly day for Vishnu
130.carry: ekadashi is a day given to vishnu
130.howItsDone: Many Hindus, especially devotees of Vishnu and Krishna, observe Ekadashi, the eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, by avoiding grains and beans or fasting, spending extra time in prayer or singing Vishnu's names, and breaking the fast the next morning; the story of King Ambarisha is often told on the day.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vasishtha named baby Rama on the eleventh day. Your line was samskaras make life's steps holy.

segments.voice: King Ambarisha loves Vishnu, and for a whole year he keeps the fast of the eleventh day. On the morning after the last one, it's time to break it. Then the sage Durvasa arrives, famous across the worlds for his temper. Ambarisha bows and invites him to eat first. Durvasa goes to bathe in the river, and takes his time. The moment for breaking the fast is slipping away. Eat before a guest, and he insults a sage. Miss the moment, and the vow is broken. What does a king do?
screen: `A YEAR OF FASTS FOR VISHNU.` → `AN ANGRY SAGE AT THE DOOR.` → `THE MOMENT IS SLIPPING.`

segments.voice: His priests advise a sip of water: it breaks the fast, and it isn't eating ahead of a guest. Durvasa comes back, sees it, and in a rage hurls a fiery demon at the king. Ambarisha doesn't move. He stands with folded hands. And Vishnu's spinning disc, the Sudarshana, burns the demon up and chases Durvasa across the worlds. Durvasa runs to Vishnu himself, who says: I am in the hands of my devotees. Go and ask him. That's the Bhagavata Purana. Here's the teaching. Ekadashi isn't a diet day. It's a day given to Vishnu, kept with love. Ekadashi means the eleventh: eka is one, dasha is ten. The Hindu calendar follows the moon. Each lunar month has a bright half, as the moon grows, and a dark half, as it shrinks, fifteen lunar days each. The eleventh day of each half is Ekadashi. So it comes about twice a month, on a different date on your wall calendar every time; that's why so many grandmothers keep a paper calendar with the days circled. Those who keep it often skip grains and beans and eat fruit, milk or nuts. Some fast fully. A few keep one Ekadashi a year without even water. The day goes to prayer, singing Vishnu's names, reading. And the fast is broken the next morning, often at a set time, just as Ambarisha tried to. A one-off vow depends on remembering. Ekadashi comes round with the moon, and twice a month it turns a whole household back toward Vishnu.

segments.voice: Shiva sits deep in meditation on his mountain, and the gods are desperate. A demon is ravaging the worlds, and only a son of Shiva can defeat him. But Shiva wants no wife and no son. So the gods send Kama, the god of desire, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers. Kama creeps close, draws, and lets an arrow fly. Shiva feels it. And the eye in the middle of his forehead, his third eye, opens. Fire pours out, and Kama is burned to ash.
screen: `ONLY SHIVA'S SON CAN WIN.` → `KAMA DRAWS HIS FLOWER BOW.` → `THE THIRD EYE OPENS.` → `ASH.`

segments.voice: That's the Shiva Purana. Kama's wife Rati weeps, and he's allowed to live on, but without a body, which is why desire is everywhere and can't be seen. And Shiva is pictured smeared with ash. Look at many devotees of Shiva today and you'll see that ash too: three lines of vibhuti, sacred ash, across the forehead. That's a tilak, the mark on the forehead, and it's the teaching today: the tilak shows whom you honor. It can be ash, cool sandalwood paste, or kumkum, a red powder made from turmeric. The shape can tell you the lineage. Three lines of ash, for Shiva. A tall U or V, often with a line down the middle, for many devotees of Vishnu and Krishna. A red dot, for many devotees of the Goddess, and others. A bindi, from bindu, a point, is worn by many women and girls, and doesn't by itself mean someone is married; in many North Indian families it's sindoor in the hair parting that marks a married woman. Why the forehead? It's the place of Shiva's third eye, and in yoga texts a center called ajna, linked with insight. Many teachers read the mark as a reminder to see from there, with the eye that burned desire away. And often it's given, not put on: by a priest after puja, or by an elder. So when a teammate asks about the smudge, there's a short, true answer. It's a tilak. It's a blessing, and it shows who I honor.
screen: `THE THIRD EYE BURNS KAMA TO ASH.` · `ASH, SANDALWOOD, RED POWDER.` · `THE SHAPE SHOWS THE LINEAGE.` · `THE PLACE OF THE THIRD EYE.` · then, large: `A TILAK MARKS THE GOD YOU HONOR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, breathe slowly, and without straining let your attention settle between your eyebrows, where a tilak would go, as if a cool fingertip of sandalwood were resting there; when the mind wanders, come back to that spot. If you pray, you can hold there the form of God you honor. If you don't, simply look out from there for a while.
Tilak. The mark on the forehead: ash, sandalwood or red powder, worn as a blessing and a sign of the god you honor. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: a tilak marks the god you honor. Right where Shiva's third eye opens. Day one hundred thirty-one, and the week is done.

132.title: Krishna turns to the window
132.hook: Kanakadasa sings outside Udupi and Krishna turns to see him; what a temple is and how to enter
132.carry: a mandir is god's house; we come as guests
132.howItsDone: Visitors to a Hindu temple remove their shoes at the entrance, often wash their hands and ring the bell, then approach the inner shrine to see and bow to the murti, visiting smaller shrines and receiving prasad; most people come and go at any time, with crowds at arti times.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiva's third eye burned desire to ash. Your line was a tilak marks the god you honor.
screen: `A TILAK MARKS THE GOD YOU HONOR.`

segments.voice: Udupi, on India's southwest coast, about five hundred years ago. A poet named Kanakadasa, a shepherd's son who sings to Krishna, comes to the great Krishna temple to see his Lord. Because of his caste, he's kept out. So he goes round to the back wall and sings to Krishna from outside. The story told at Udupi says the image of Krishna turned around to face him, and the wall cracked open into a window, so the two could see each other. That window is still called Kanaka's window.
screen: `A POET KEPT OUT.` → `HE SINGS AT THE BACK WALL.` → `KRISHNA TURNS AROUND.` → `KANAKA'S WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Notice what the story takes for granted: Krishna is home. That's the teaching today. The Hindi word mandir comes from the Sanskrit mandira: a dwelling, a house. A temple is understood as a home where God lives, in the murti, the sacred image, which has been ritually installed, like the clay Ganesha you met long ago, and is cared for every day: woken, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night. You're not walking into an auditorium. You're visiting someone's house, and God is the host. That's why everybody first takes off their shoes; there's usually a rack by the door. Many wash their hands, then ring the bell at the entrance, the ghanta, to say you've arrived. At the heart of the temple is the garbhagriha, the womb-house: small, often dark, lit by lamps, with the main image inside. In many temples only priests go in; everyone else stands at the threshold, looks, and bows. There's often no single service: people come and go, though arti times draw a crowd. A few quiet customs: dress modestly, don't point your feet at the shrine, and ask before taking photos. Many temples welcome visitors of any background; some admit only Hindus. And Kanakadasa's story adds one more thing: the house belongs to God, and God turns toward whoever comes with love. So if you're nervous at the steps, do what a guest does anywhere. Shoes off, watch, and follow.
screen: `MANDIR — A DWELLING, A HOUSE.` · `GOD IS THE HOST.` · `SHOES OFF, RING THE BELL.` · `BOW AT THE THRESHOLD.` · then, large: `A MANDIR IS GOD'S HOUSE; WE COME AS GUESTS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and walk in slowly: at the steps, take off your shoes and feel the cool floor, maybe rinse your hands, then ring the bell and listen to it fade. Walk toward the lamplight, to a small, dim doorway with the image inside, lit by flames, and stop at the threshold. Put your hands together if you'd like, and just stand there, a guest in the house.
Mandir. The Hindu temple: a house where God lives and is cared for every day, and where you enter as a guest, shoes off. Today's word.

133.title: Dhruva opens his eyes
133.hook: Dhruva holds Vishnu in his heart, then opens his eyes to find him there; darshan
133.carry: darshan is seeing god, and being seen
133.howItsDone: Hindus go to temples for darshan, standing before the murti with folded hands to see the deity and be seen in return; many also speak of taking darshan of saints, sacred rivers and holy places.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna turned to the window to see Kanakadasa. Your line was a mandir is God's house; we come as guests.
screen: `A MANDIR IS GOD'S HOUSE; WE COME AS GUESTS.`

segments.voice: A five-year-old prince named Dhruva tries to climb onto his father's lap. His stepmother pulls him away: you're not my son, so you don't belong there. If you want a place like that, go and pray to Vishnu. So he does. He walks into the forest and, taught by a sage, sits and holds Vishnu's form in his heart, month after month, until even the gods feel the weight of his prayer. Then one day, the form he's been seeing inside suddenly disappears. Startled, Dhruva opens his eyes.
screen: `PULLED OFF HIS FATHER'S LAP.` → `INTO THE FOREST.` → `VISHNU HELD IN HIS HEART.` → `THEN HE OPENS HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: And there in front of him stands Vishnu: the same form he'd held inside, now outside, looking back at him. The boy is so overcome he can't speak, until Vishnu touches his cheek with his conch shell and praise pours out of him. That's the Bhagavata Purana, and Dhruva, it says, was given the pole star, the one star that doesn't move. That moment has a name, and it's the teaching today: darshan. It comes from the Sanskrit root drish, to see. In a temple it means to stand before God and look, and to be looked at in return. That second half is the surprise. Many Hindus understand the murti as truly inhabited, so the seeing goes both ways. That's why the eyes of the image matter so much: often large and bright, sometimes silver. In the rites that install a new image, there is a moment for opening its eyes, and after that, the image is said to see. In some temples a curtain covers the shrine at times, and when it opens, the crowd leans forward: darshan! Hands come together. Some say a name under their breath. Some just look. You can take darshan of a holy person, a sacred river, a mountain. And the classical schools of Hindu philosophy are called darshanas, ways of seeing. So that's why people wait six hours in line for three seconds at the front. They aren't only looking at God. Like Dhruva, they're being seen. Three seconds can be enough, if you actually look.
screen: `DHRUVA OPENS HIS EYES: VISHNU IS THERE.` · `DARSHAN — FROM DRISH, TO SEE.` · `THE EYES ARE OPENED IN THE RITE.` · `THE CURTAIN OPENS: DARSHAN!` · then, large: `DARSHAN IS SEEING GOD, AND BEING SEEN.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze rest softly on an image that matters to you, the murti in your corner, a picture of a deity, a photo of a teacher or someone you love, or simply the sky out the window, especially on the eyes if there are eyes. Don't analyze it; just look, the way you'd look at someone you've missed. Then turn it around and stay with both: what would it be like to be seen like this, fully, without judgment?
Darshan. Seeing: standing before God, a holy person or a holy place, to see and to be seen in return. Today's word.
screen: `DARSHAN — today's word`.
